title: Houthis v. Saudi Arabia: Round 2. This time it's regional. - Responsible Statecraft
content:
After fresh clashes with the Yemeni military group, Riyadh finds itself at the center of overlapping wars and skirmishes, including Iran and Iraq On July 28, Saudi air defenses shot down drones launched from Iraqi territory by “Iran-affiliated terrorist militias,” a Saudi ministry of defense statement read. The attacks targeted oil facilities in the Eastern Province and at the capital, Riyadh, itself. Days earlier, Houthi forces in Yemen said they had hit “sensitive” oil transport sites linking the Eastern Province to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu. Satellite images showed smoke over the kingdom's most important oil infrastructure. Both attacks come amid a wider escalation that began with the Houthis’ declared naval blockade of Saudi ports, followed by strikes on several ships and an exchange of missile fire with the kingdom. The Houthis say they will lift the blockade only once Saudi Arabia ends what they call a “blockade” on Yemen; they also have separate financial demands, chiefly, a demand for public-sector salaries and a share of the revenue from Yemen oil industry, which is located in territory held by the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government of Yemen. Saudi Arabia is now being squeezed from three directions in the widening U.S.-Iran war — Iraq to its northeast, Yemen to its southwest, and Iran to its east. (On July 18, Tehran struck Prince Sultan Air Base near Riyadh, its first direct hit on Saudi soil in nearly four months.) To understand why this matters beyond the price of oil, it helps to picture the crises as a set of nesting dolls. The innermost doll is Yemen’s own civil war: a decade-old fight between the Houthis (officially known as Ansar Allah), who rule the populous north from Sana’a, and Yemen’s internationally recognized government, formally led by a body called the Presidential Leadership Council. The roots of this war trace to the 2011 Arab Spring revolution, which toppled Yemen’s long-serving president and left a power vacuum the Houthis moved to fill, seizing Sana’a in 2014. Saudi Arabia and a coalition of partners intervened in 2015 with the explicit aim of reversing that takeover and restoring the internationally recognized government, and the war has continued in one form or another ever since. The middle doll is Saudi Arabia’s broader rivalry with Iran, a contest for regional leadership that has run since Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution, when Tehran’s new theocratic government began exporting a revolutionary, Shia-inflected challenge to the Gulf’s Sunni monarchies. Since the Houthis’ seizure of Sana’a in September 2014, Iran has absorbed the group into what it calls its “axis of resistance,” supplying it with weapons, funding and technical know-how, turning Yemen into an arena of proxy war between Tehran and Riyadh. The outer doll is the American-Iranian war itself, now in its sixth month, which has all but closed the Strait of Hormuz and pushed oil prices to record highs. This conflict set the other two into motion. Since March 2022, an unofficial truce kept Yemen’s civil war, the Houthi-Saudi war, and the Saudi-Iranian rivalry in Yemen quiet even as the outer dolls rattled. That calm helped pave the way for a Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023. What is new, and dangerous, is that all are now moving together. This month saw the fiercest clashes in years between Houthi fighters and government-aligned forces in the southern province of Dhale, which left dozens killed on both sides. Briefing reporters in Riyadh — where much of the official Yemeni government’s leadership operates — Yemen's new foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, said, “at the end of the day, we are prepared for any escalations.” She also warned that the “Houthis want to copy the Iran experience in Hormuz.” The trigger for current tensions was a July 3 Iranian Mahan Air flight, which landed in Houthi-held Sana’a to collect a delegation traveling to Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s funeral, the first such direct flight in more than a decade. Riyadh had long blocked exactly this kind of corridor, fearing it would be used to send weapons or military advisers to the Houthis. That fear proved well-founded, according to Reuters, which reported that the return flight on July 13th brought with it Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps personnel, along with missile and drone components. The Houthis have denied the accusations. Subscribe now to our weekly round-up and don't miss a beat with your favorite RS contributors and reporters, as well as staff analysis, opinion, and news promoting a positive, non-partisan vision of U.S. foreign policy. Yemen’s internationally recognized government, backed by the Saudi-led coalition, has always treated the country’s airspace as remaining under its own legal authority. When that plane returned on July 13th, the government struck the airport runway to stop it landing again. The aircraft diverted to Hodeidah instead. That strike was not a unilateral decision. According to Axios, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman personally sought and received President Trump’s backing for the operation in a phone call days beforehand. Riyadh, it appeared, knew it was gambling with the Houthi truce and risked inflaming the already tense standoff between the U.S. and Iran, and wanted American cover before it moved. The Houthis retaliated within hours, firing missiles at Abha Airport in southern Saudi Arabia, the first direct strike on the kingdom in four years. All of this demonstrates how entangled Yemen’s civil war has become with the wider U.S.-Iran war. Iranian officials made this connection explicit while the Houthi delegation was in Tehran for Khamenei’s funeral. Ali Akbar Velayati, the supreme leader’s adviser, told the group that the siege of Yemen “must end immediately.” Parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, praised Sana’a’s loyalty, stating that Ansar Allah “always stood by the resistance in defending Lebanon and Palestine.” Iran’s foreign ministry has stuck to a more measured public tone. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there is “no military solution to the issue of Yemen,” and the ministry spokesman called for the U.N.-brokered 2023 roadmap to be “fully implemented.” However, this diplomatic call quietly endorses the Houthi narrative. Both officials characterized Sana’a as being under "siege," and under “continued blockade,” a clear acceptance of the Houthi framing of Saudi restrictions. Saudi Arabia, notably, has not pointed blame at Iran directly for inflaming tensions in Yemen. Instead, Yemeni officials have leveled these accusations. Yemen’s information minister, Moammar al-Iryani, stated outright that Houthi military decisions are now “more closely tied to directives from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard.” Riyadh has let its own client government make the accusations it avoids voicing directly, perhaps because naming Iran directly would foreclose the diplomatic space Riyadh still wants to maintain. That restraint would fit a broader pattern: Saudi Arabia has reportedly been keen to see the U.S.-Iran tensions resolved diplomatically rather than militarily, having already rejected Washington’s request to use Saudi airspace and bases for Project Freedom, the U.S. plan to escort ships through Hormuz. Riyadh, in other words, is hedging on multiple fronts at once. It is avoiding a total rupture with Tehran even as it fights Tehran’s allies on its southern flank and in Iraq, where it conducted airstrikes on Iran-aligned groups with the U.S. on July 28. That hedging leaves the door to de-escalation narrowed, but not fully shut. Oman, the traditional backchannel in Yemen’s civil war, said on July 23 that it was coordinating with Saudi Arabia, “Yemeni parties,” and the U.N.’s special envoy for Yemen to try to revive the stalled political process. That same weekend, Omani officials were in Tehran running a parallel negotiation on the Strait of Hormuz, shuttling between Iranian and American positions on ship-routing and transit fees. Oman is, in effect, trying to broker both of the region's thorniest disputes at once — a measure of how much regional diplomacy now runs through Muscat, and of how intertwined the conflicts have become. But diplomacy is losing ground. Reuters reported last week that Western officials involved in the Yemen mediation are increasingly pessimistic about reaching a negotiated resolution. Meanwhile, Houthi rhetoric towards its Yemeni rivals and Riyadh has grown increasingly fiery, and Saudi Arabia has made clear that attacks on its territory and tankers won't go unanswered. Encouraged by Ukraine’s sustained advances in drone warfare, Western media is abuzz with the idea that Kyiv just might be able to defeat Russia after more than four years of bitter fighting. In May, TIME hailed Ukraine’s drone industry as giving Kyiv “the cards to win without U.S. help.” Last month, CNN lauded Ukrainian drone strikes near Moscow as “a likely turning point” in the war. Earlier this month, Defense One even framed the conflict as a settled matter with the headline “How Ukraine won the first great robot war.” Former President Juan Orlando Hernández, the convicted drug trafficker pardoned by President Donald Trump last December, flew triumphantly home to Honduras on Sunday in full, ambitious glory. He stepped off a private plane wearing a crisp white shirt, looking clean as the driven snow, a far cry from the handcuffs he wore the last time he stood on Honduran soil. Hernández's return, both astonishing and chilling, underscores Trump's ability to use his pardon power to undermine the rule of law both at home and abroad — intervening in a sovereign nation to push it further to the right and land yet another blow in the long arc of destructive U.S. intervention in Honduras. Trump's use of a presidential pardon to empower the forces of greed and repression in Honduras is entirely unprecedented. But it's just a new tool in the imperial toolbox. As Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky arrives in Washington, much indicates that he is no longer merely trying to draw greater American support into its war against Russia. Increasingly, it appears to be pursuing something far more consequential: merging the Ukraine war with the U.S.-Iran conflict into a single strategic theater. The distinction matters. If the two wars become one, Ukraine ceases to be merely a recipient of American military assistance and instead becomes a direct participant in Washington's war with Tehran. By the same token, the United States would no longer simply be Ukraine's principal arms supplier. It would become an active belligerent against Russia through a conflict that stretches from the Black Sea to the Caspian. title: A Summer Al Fresco Afternoon at V. Sattui Winery in Napa Valley - San Francisco Bay Times
content: Driving north along Napa Valley’s Highway 29, you pass a plethora of imposing wineries with lengthy, winding driveways and majestic buildings situated in picture-perfect vineyards. Then you see it … a sprawling lawn dotted with smiling visitors at picnic tables, children running around laughing, and dogs frolicking in the grass. In the background is a beautiful old stone building surrounded by vines. You think to yourself, this spot looks fun. Turns out, you’re right. This joyous place is V. Sattui Winery. After a decades-long career visiting wineries around the globe, I rarely wax poetic and it takes something very special to inspire such rhapsodizing. My recent visit to V. Sattui in Napa Valley has me doing just that. I hadn’t been to the property in nearly 20 years. It’s a staple in Napa Valley, but I was always chasing the latest rising-star winery. I finally decided it was time to revisit this historic destination on its 50th anniversary landmark. Their story began in San Francisco where Italian immigrant, Vittorio Sattui, opened a small winery in 1885. Prohibition shut their doors but not their dreams. In 1975, Vittorio’s great-grandson, Dario Sattui, brought the family business back to life in Napa Valley with the goal of sharing the Italian lifestyle connecting wine, food, family, and friends. Stepping into their bustling, recently renovated market, Mercato del Gusto, is a feast for the senses. It’s sleek and modern, but you still feel like you’re in the old winery building. It smells delicious due to the numerous bar and food areas serving an extensive menu of sandwiches, cheeses, desserts, and more. At one tasting bar I spoke with a group of women celebrating birthdays, at another was a couple toasting their weekend away. The atmosphere was electric. It was there I met Tom Davies, the passionate, long-time President and Managing Partner of the winery. His love of V. Sattui comes shining through in his wide grin. “It’s not a job, it’s my life,” he has said. Along with Director of Winemaking, Jason Moravec, and Michelin-star Executive Estate Chef, Stefano Masanti, I was treated to an al fresco afternoon on the patio sampling award-winning wines, noshing on custom charcuterie platters, and even ending with house-crafted chocolates and gelato. To shine a light on V. Sattui’s commitment to accessibility for all wine lovers, they have started offering a free three-wine tasting flight every Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. In the current hyper-priced Napa Valley, this is a savvy move. Not only has it increased their business on typically slow tasting days, but it has also endeared itself even more to V. Sattui’s fans old and new. Because V. Sattui Winery was founded on the concept of sharing wine in the context of everyday life, the way to buy their wares is by visiting. As Tom Davies said to me, “Being direct it’s about the experience. In the old days, our tastings were held on a redwood board spread over two wine barrels. From the beginning, we wanted to make small lots of delicious wine and sell it directly to consumers.” V. Sattui’s roster of wine offerings is vast and includes recognized wines such as cabernet sauvignon, pinot noir, zinfandel, sauvignon blanc, and chardonnay, but they also produce limited bottlings of unique wines. Their lineup includes reds such as grenache, malbec, and petite sirah, along with whites ranging from albariño to sémillon, a variety of rieslings, and even sparkling and sweet wines. There’s always something new to discover. If you want to try the V. Sattui wines, you can buy them online (https://www.vsattui.com/), but I recommend visiting and getting the full experience. Bring an empty stomach and an appetite for palate-pleasing adventure with you! Here are two standout bottlings from my recent visit: 2022 V. Sattui Cabernet Franc, Alexander Valley, Sonoma County $80 As a fan of cabernet franc, I’m constantly on the lookout for new bottles of the classic variety. A centuries-old vine from the Bordeaux region of France, it’s one of the parents of the famed red grape, cabernet sauvignon (white grape sauvignon blanc being the other). V. Sattui’s expression showcases sultry aromas of dark fruits, tea leaves, and rose petals. Once you sip it, the earthy, savory notes are layered with a lush yet lovely texture. It is a beauty to drink now or to cellar for up to a decade. 2025 V. Sattui Chenin Blanc, Los Carneros, Napa Valley $38 Looking for a perfect white to quench your thirst regardless of season? This one is it. Chenin blanc is a grape known in France’s Loire Valley but also in a few pockets in California where it’s grown. V. Sattui’s vineyard in the cool Los Carneros growing area, straddling Napa and Sonoma, gives the vines plenty of time to ripen while maintaining acidity and freshness. Crisp and juicy with hints of citrus and orange blossom, it is alluring to smell and lip-smackingly good to drink. Pair it alongside grilled fish, roast chicken, or spicy curry. You Gotta Try This!” and the national series “100 Days, Drinks, Dishes & Destinations.” www.LeslieSbrocco.com

title: Rio Ngumoha goal settles Liverpool v Wrexham clash in New York - Liverpool FC
content:
A late, deflected Rio Ngumoha goal helped Liverpool edge out Wrexham 1-0 in their pre-season fixture in New York on Wednesday evening. The 17-year-old had an effort take a ricochet inside the area that looped the ball over the goalkeeper and into the net with 15 minutes left, to settle the contest at Yankee Stadium in the Reds’ favour. It means Andoni Iraola’s side have won both outings on their USA tour so far, with a further match against Leeds United in Chicago to follow on Sunday. After the 4-2 victory over Sunderland in Iraola’s first game in charge in Nashville last weekend, the head coach made a handful of changes to the starting line-up, including berths for Milos Kerkez and Dominik Szoboszlai, with the latter wearing the captain’s armband. Liverpool could have taken the lead inside three minutes at Yankee Stadium. It was Szoboszlai who played a threaded pass into the path of Harvey Elliott in midfield, who in turn slipped Josh Abe in behind. The youngster’s effort was repelled by former Reds stopper Danny Ward, however. Shortly after, Lewis Koumas went early with a low shot across goal from just outside the area that didn’t evade the bottom corner by much at all. At the other end, Wrexham threatened when Sam Smith pounced on a ricochet inside the box, but saw his drive at close range deflect off Ifeanyi Ndukwe and spin over the crossbar. The forward was involved again when he got a touch to a bouncing ball from a long pass forward, which had Giorgi Mamardashvili advancing from his goalline. The ’keeper managed to get his body in the way of the ball to eliminate the danger. On 33 minutes, Koumas asked in vain for a penalty when he claimed he had been tripped by Dan Scarr after attempting to meet Szoboszlai’s through ball, but those appeals were waved away. Four changes were made by Iraola during the break, but Wrexham had an early chance as a cross to the back post from the left dropped for Ryan Longman, but he could only skew wide as he stretched to reach the ball. At the other end, tenacious play by Koumas kept a ball alive on the left before he found Elliott on the edge of the box. His swipe at goal was parried by Ward as it made its way towards the bottom corner. The goalkeeper was called into action again soon after, getting behind a crisp Szoboszlai touch and hit from just outside the area. A Nathan Broadhead thump from distance required a diving save from Mamardashvili as Wrexham threatened, but Liverpool took the lead with 15 minutes remaining. Szoboszlai rolled the ball to Ngumoha midway inside the opposition half. He ran at a back-peddling defensive line before arriving into the box, where a low shot took a deflection off Lewis Brunt and looped over substitute stopper Callum Burton. The Championship side spurned a late chance to grab a draw when Kieffer Moore scuffed over from Brunt’s delivery at point-blank range, ensuring it’s two from two for Liverpool so far on their tour of the USA. Seaside: When client AI use can sink work product protection Massachusetts trial court holds that certain uses of AI to generate legal documents could compromise attorney work product protection. In its June 16, 2026, decision in Earl Wade Shealy Jr. v. Seaside Investments, LLC, No. 2684CV00799-BLS2, the Suffolk County Superior Court’s Business Litigation Session (Squires-Lee, J.) compelled production of documents that the plaintiff’s romantic partner had generated using ChatGPT. The court held that, on the facts before it, neither AI queries for legal assistance nor the resulting output were protected work product when made by someone who is not a party’s representative and not at the direction of counsel—even though the party was represented and the materials were created in anticipation of litigation. Although the trial court’s order is not binding on other courts, the decision offers an early and instructive window into how judges may treat AI-assisted materials in discovery. The dispute arose from alleged breaches of an agreement on the purchase and sale of a gas station in Boston’s South End neighborhood. The plaintiff, Earl Wade Shealy, Jr., alleges that the defendants defaulted on a promissory note and loan agreement by failing to pay as required under the agreements’ terms. Seaside Investments LLC responded by sending a letter to Shealy also alleging default. Shealy, in turn, forwarded the document to his partner, Debbi Fields. Fields then uploaded the documents to ChatGPT, generated a response letter and other documents using the AI tool, and emailed the output back to Shealy. No attorney was involved in Fields’s use of ChatGPT. Fields testified she was merely “like a Xerox,” assisting with “providing a paperwork flow.” Defendants moved to compel production of (i) the ChatGPT communications and output, and (ii) documents relating to Shealy’s financial ability to prepay the note. Plaintiffs argued that the AI-generated documents were prepared in anticipation of litigation and therefore were protected under the work product doctrine. The court’s decision turned on an analysis of three major requirements for the work product doctrine, which protects (1) documents and tangible things (2) prepared by or for another party or by or for that party’s representative (3) in anticipation of litigation or for trial. The court held that Fields, as Shealy’s romantic partner, was not a “representative” under the work product doctrine. The types of persons whose documents are protected under Mass. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(3), including a party’s “attorney, consultant, surety, indemnitor, insurer, or agent,” do not include a friend or partner with “absolutely no substantive connection to the litigation or to plaintiffs’ counsel.” Expanding the definition to cover such individuals, the court reasoned, would not “enhance the vitality of an adversary system” and would “expand the work product doctrine without meaningful limitation.” Plaintiffs cited two recent federal decisions—Morgan v. V2X, Inc., No. 25–CV–01991–SKC–MDB, at *2 (D. Colo. Mar. 30, 2026) and Warner v. Gilbarco, Inc., 820 F. Supp. 3d 629, 636 (E.D. Mich. 2026)—both of which held AI-generated materials are subject to work product protection. The court distinguished those cases because both involved pro se litigants using AI as both party and advocate. Here, plaintiffs were represented by “sophisticated, capable counsel.” The court found the case more akin to United States v. Heppner, 820 F. Supp. 3d 292 (S.D.N.Y. 2026), in which AI documents generated by a represented defendant on his own “volition” did not merit work product protection because they were not prepared at the “behest” of counsel and did not reflect “counsel’s strategy.” The court’s holding on this issue of first impression: Neither the queries of AI programs for legal assistance by a party’s romantic partner nor the AI output are protected from disclosure under the work product doctrine unless performed at the direction of counsel. The court further held that ChatGPT’s output does not qualify as opinion work product, which is discoverable only in extreme circumstances. As the court stated: “AI is a tool, not a person. Nothing about what ChatGPT produces discloses the ‘mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, or legal theories of an attorney or other representative of a party concerning the litigation.’” While Massachusetts courts have already confronted AI—most notably in sanctioning attorneys for citing fabricated, AI-generated cases (such as Judge Brian A. Davis’ 2024 warning to the “broader bar” in Smith v. Farwell, No. 2282CV01197 (Mass. Super. Ct. Feb. 12, 2024))—Shealy appears to be among the first to reach AI through the work product doctrine, and one of the earliest anywhere to do so involving a represented party. The court’s reasoning sends a strong signal: the work product shield may not extend to AI use by someone who is not a party’s “representative” and who is acting outside counsel’s oversight. Companies[1] and individuals would be well served to keep the following in mind: Route litigation-related AI use through counsel. The court’s favorable citation to United States v. Heppner is a strong signal that work product protection may turn on whether AI is used at the “direction of counsel.” Parties are well advised to involve counsel before using AI tools to draft or analyze litigation-related documents. Under the court’s reasoning, even a party’s own, self-initiated AI use could fall outside the doctrine’s protection. Think twice before sharing litigation documents with non-attorneys for AI analysis. Under Shealy, sending legal documents to a spouse, partner, family member, or friend who then uses AI to generate analysis, or draft responses may carry no privilege or work product protection. A close family relationship may not change the analysis: the marital privilege protects confidential communications between spouses, and the court’s reasoning suggests it may not reach documents a spouse creates by feeding materials into a public AI tool. Similar questions could arise as to parents, children, and other relatives, and the risk that such materials are ordered produced is a real one. Address AI use during disputes in internal policies. Organizations are well positioned to get ahead of this issue by making clear when employees should consult counsel before using AI tools to analyze or respond to legal matters, including demand letters, regulatory inquiries, and contracts in dispute. Revisit litigation hold and preservation procedures. Companies are well served to look at whether their litigation hold notices reach AI-generated content, and whether employees understand any obligations to preserve AI interactions relating to disputes, since opposing parties may seek their production. Favor counsel-directed or enterprise AI tools for litigation work. The decision is not a reason to avoid AI, but a strong reason to be deliberate about how it is used. Where counsel directs the AI use, or where the work runs through an enterprise platform with appropriate confidentiality and data-handling protections rather than a public chatbot, AI-assisted materials stand a far better chance of qualifying as protected work product. Federal law enforcement are abusing people who are simply exercising their First Amendment rights. Since the President Trump began his second term, people, regardless of their immigration status, have faced relentless attacks for exercising their First Amendment rights. 13 of our affiliates’ clients were retaliated against for exercising their First Amendment rights across 5 states and Washington, D.C. The ACLU of New Jersey’s client was operating a mobile health clinic outside an ICE detention center where active protests were taking place inside and outside the facility — then she was attacked by ICE. Norma Bowe, is a grandmother, professor of public health at Kean University, and registered nurse who operates a mobile clinic that provides free medical services to people across northern New Jersey. Since May 2025, her clinic has regularly stationed at Delaney Hall to support families visiting loved ones in the detention center. “ICE agents are acting like they have impunity and are inflicting harm however and whenever they want; without accountability, more people will get hurt and die. ICE must be held responsible.” - Dr. Norma Bowe Throughout the protests related to the detainees’ hunger strike, she was operating her mobile health clinic. One day, an ICE agent grabbed Norma and violently threw her to the ground. ICE is incarcerating people in dangerous facilities, where people detained are subjected to systematic abuse and egregious medical neglect. Right now, there are a record 65,000+ people in ICE detention facilities nationwide as the Trump administration rushes to expand the ICE detention machine fueled by the for-profit private prison industry. For decades, ICE detention has been notorious for horrific rights violations, medical abuse, and utter disregard for the dignity of people in custody. 14 of our affiliates’ clients experienced abuses in ICE detention, and their stories are only the tip of the iceberg. Two of the ACLU of Louisiana’s clients were denied access to medication, forced into physical labor, subject to severe physical and sexual abuse, and retaliated against, including by being placed in solitary confinement. Mario Garcia-Valenzuela and Luis Renteria Gonzalez were detained for nearly two and three years, respectively, at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana. They suffered forced labor, physical abuse, sexual abuse, inadequate medical care, and severe retaliation by the facility’s staff, including placement in solitary confinement. “I’m speaking out now because ICE needs to be held accountable for what happened to me. And because I don't want this to happen to anyone else.” - Luis Renteria-Gonzalez As trans men, Mario and Luis were forced to perform intense manual labor in an off-the-books program that targeted transgender and masculine-presenting LGBTQ+ detained people. They were assaulted by officers and suffered serious injuries from forced labor. When Luis and Mario filed complaints about this abuse, they were held in solitary confinement for weeks, where they were denied food and access to their attorney. Mario was repeatedly denied his seizure medication, causing him to have at least 10 seizures in a one-month period, leading to his hospitalization. They both also experienced and witnessed sexual assault and harassment, including being forced to stand guard while an officer raped a detained woman. And when their families came to visit them in detention, officers stalked their families in the nearby town. ICE and federal law enforcement are racially profiling and arresting U.S. citizens unlawfully. Federal agents’ actions have not only harmed people without permanent legal status, but also U.S. citizens. In fact, more than half of our affiliates’ clients (29) were U.S. citizens harmed by federal law enforcement — and of those, 12 U.S. citizen clients were racially profiled and unlawfully detained. One of the ACLU of North Carolina’s clients, a U.S. citizen, was racially profiled and put into a unmarked SUV before federal agents released him, bleeding, on the side of the road. Willy Wender Aceituno, a U.S. citizen in North Carolina, was on his way into a restaurant when four armed and masked immigration agents surrounded him, pushed him against an agency’s vehicle, and forced him to provide identification to confirm his citizenship. Mr. Aceituno provided his Real ID driver’s license, and after confirming his citizenship, the agents walked away. But moments later after returning to his truck, agency vehicles pulled in front and behind him to block his exit. While he began to record, the agents shattered his window and attempted to grab his phone before holding Mr. Aceituno in a headlock and pulling him from his truck. He was thrown onto the pavement, which was covered in broken glass, and he suffered bleeding cuts all over his body. Mr. Aceituno was handcuffed, placed in an unmarked SUV, and driven away from the scene. He kept repeating that he was a citizen while the agents continued to tell him to “shut up.” Eventually, the SUV stopped, an agent took Mr. Aceituno’s wallet from his front pocket and confirmed that he was a citizen with no criminal record. The agents released Mr. Aceituno on the side of the road, still bleeding and 2 miles away from his truck. As these stories show, federal agents’ abuses are not limited to any one population, demographic, or surge. The ACLU’s new report, Agents of Chaos and Cruelty, underscores how federal agents' conduct has harmed citizens and noncitizens alike in states across the country. The report examines immigration enforcement incidents in eight states and found that over 400 of the more than 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents examined involved misconduct by immigration agents. Though the incidents examined represent a small fraction of total reported enforcement activity in 2025, the pattern across eight states makes clear that excessive force, racial profiling, intimidation, and abuse by both federal officials and state and local law enforcement are paramount to the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant agenda.

title: King v. United States – Challenging National Guard Members’ Violent Seizure of a Veteran - ACLU of DC
content: Anna King is a retired U.S. Army captain and an Iraq War veteran, receiving a Purple Heart and a Bronze Star for her service. On May 8, 2026, she was at her home when three National Guard members walked through her gated patio and seized her, shoving her toward the ground, grabbing her arms, and applying handcuffs so tightly that they ruptured ligaments in her wrist, requiring surgery. The Guard members contended that they detained King because she assaulted them two days earlier; but this assertion is baseless and King was never charged with the alleged offense. Instead, the only apparent reason for the Guard members’ decision to target her was her speech, via the prominent signs in her window criticizing their presence in the District. In conjunction with the law firm Levy Firestone Muse LLP, we filed an administrative Federal Tort Claims Act complaint with the Idaho National Guard (which employs several of the Guard members involved) and the Department of Defense to vindicate King’s rights. title: Ronald V. Paulseen Obituary Jul 29, 2026 - Cozine Memorial Group
content:
Ronald Virgel Paulseen was born in McPherson, Kansas April 8, 1949 in the home of Paul Virgel Wanigold Paulseen and Elva Olivia Ledell Paulseen loving parents who showed he and his sister Virdell Paulseen Shay what really mattered in life. Ron was raised in a strong Lutheran home around a lot of extended aunts, uncles, first and second cousins. He was given tenants in life that would serve him well, a passion to work hard, a desire to do things right the first time and an interest in serving people. His childhood was spent working alongside his dad at Paulseen Construction Company; there Ron would learn to make just about anything with wood. Ron poured every free moment into his life as a Boy Scout and lived life proud to have achieved his Eagle Scout. He worked at the Peterson lumberyard in high school but headed off to college at his dear Bethany in Lindsborg just 14 miles from home. He studied hard knowing exactly how much work at the lumberyard it took to pay for each course credit. While studying at Bethany College he met the love of his life, Jenny Peck. He graduated Magna Cum Laude in three and half years. He continued his work at the lumberyard to get his bride to be through school. They married on December 27, 1970, followed by Jenny’s graduation from Bethany College in spring of 1972 and settled in Wichita, Kansas. Ron always called his life “divinely guided”, and his first and only job after the lumberyard kept him in awe of that thought throughout his life. On April 17, 1972 he signed his contract with the New York Life, a decision 22 year old Ron could never imagine the impact it would have on him. The business was extremely difficult, especially for someone who had just moved to the biggest town he ever been in and knew no one. Ron was extremely determined to succeed and did everything he was told to do, excelling immediately. Throughout his 50 year career, Ron became internationally known as one of the most enjoyed speakers on The Million Dollar Round Table main platform and was a member of the highly coveted Top of the Table for over four decades. He was known for making complex concepts simple. He was a leader, serving as president of several prestigious organizations, The Agents Advisory Council, The Nautilus Group and NYLARC, the largest agent-owned reinsurance company in the country. His career allowed Ron to meet the most special people to him, clients, who became dear friends and colleagues who became his brothers. He and Jenny raised two children, Aeramy (Porter) and Brandon and have three grandchildren, Trip Porter, Hadley Porter and Brann Paulseen. All who met Ron knew his family meant more to him than anything. He beamed with pride telling anyone he met about his kids and grandchildren. He was an exemplary father who gave of himself more than any child could ever ask. He never missed an event and was always available to listen, to laugh and to love through the good, the bad, and the ugly. To his children he was more than their dad, he was their best friend, confidant, mentor, and biggest champion- the greatest gift a child could ever receive. In 1998 he purchased a dream come true for him, El Rancho del Ronnie V ~ a treasured property equidistant from his home in McPherson and Lindsborg, the town where he and Jenny met. This became his refuge, where he would go to recharge weekly. He had a full function shop equipped with many of the tools from his father’s construction business. He built countless sets of shelves for his kids’ homes, his garage, his office, they were such a gift! He spent hours upon hours mowing and grooming his property – it was impeccable, the most beautiful in the county. He and Jenny entertained family, friends, colleagues, held board meetings, reunions, study group meetings, girl’s trips, guy’s trips and even Brandon and Lindsay’s wedding. To those who have had the honor to experience El Rancho del Ronnie V we hope those memories will stay with you for life and inspire you to live like infamous Ronnie V. Ron was a great philanthropist and loved to share his time, treasure and talent. He served on the board of trustees at Wichita Collegiate School for 15 years and always sang their praises telling everyone, “Jenny and I paid for two educations but got four”. He also served as a board member and benefactor of Bethany College. He daily improved the lives of others with countless acts of generosity. The world has lost a mortal angel, but he can now do what he loves most, serve others as their guardian angel for eternity. As written by Ron’s oldest grandchild, Trip, in his senior Good Life paper, “Respect is ultimately the end goal of a good life. Not because you will achieve high positions, friendships or success, but it means you have fulfilled your duties through good and genuine actions.” This WAS Ron Paulseen. He was preceded in death by his dear parents, Paul Virgel Wanigold Paulseen and Elva Olivia Ledell Paulseen of McPherson, KS. title: The V-10 Engine May Be Gone, But These Cars Will Never Be Forgotten - Road & Track
content: We love a good V-10 engine, and these are the best of the bunch. New production cars that use V-10 power are no more. That train left with the departure of the Lamborghini Huracán and the Audi R8, which means this list is full of greatest hits from the past. Many are supercars, but there’s the occasional odd duck in the mix, too, including a few oddball SUVs and pickup trucks. These are the best V-10-powered cars ever made. The Viper may be dead now, but it’s the car we think of first when it comes to legendary, V-10-powered machines. The track-ready ACR version is a beast on the circuit, with a big 645-hp 8.4-liter V-10 and comically large aero. Prices for the ultra-barebones first-gen are still within reason, but the fifth-gen has skyrocketed in value since the Viper went out of production. No matter which version of the Lamborghini Huracán you prefer, you're getting a naturally aspirated 5.2-liter V-10 that shrieks its way to a high redline. This mid-engine Lamborghini has talents that span from the racetrack with the STO to excellence off-road with the Sterrato. Its successor, the hybrid Temerario, loses two cylinders and tacks on a couple of turbochargers. The Audi R8 was initially offered with a V-8, but not long after launching, it added a 5.2-liter V-10. Throughout its long production run, the R8 tended to follow the Lamborghini Huracán. We finally saw Audi’s incredible supercar go out of production after 2023 production concluded, but just like Lamborghini, Audi has a twin-turbo V-8 successor with its Nuvolari. Before the Huracán, the Gallardo held court as the entry-level Lambo supercar. This angular, mid-engine success story produced 493 horsepower and matured across 10 model years, birthing dozens of iterations and special editions. They’re still not cheap, but you can pick one up at the bottom of the market for around the $100,000 mark today. Read our 20-year retrospective review of the Gallardo The Porsche Carrera GT is one of the most special Porsches ever produced. You can trace its engine’s lineage back to Le Mans and F1 cars, which the sound should remind you of instantly. The 5.7-liter V-10 paired with a manual transmission is a combination for the ages, one its 918 successor even struggled to compete against. This particular Porsche is one of the greatest sports cars ever made in addition to being one of the greatest V-10s. WHY THE CARRERA GT IS STILL PORSCHE'S GREATEST SUPERCAR The LFA makes a strong argument for being the best-sounding car of all time. Lexus teamed up with Yamaha's musical instrument division, and they tuned the LFA's engine note like it was a guitar. Described by Toyota engineers as a "roar of an angel," we agree wholeheartedly. The 553 horsepower seems almost secondary. Almost. The LFA name is being revived for an EV to come in the future, but we’ll never forget this V-10 masterpiece. The E60-generation BMW M5 is perhaps one of the scarier used-car purchases one can make today, but that doesn’t make it any less tempting. Bellowing up to a redline of 8250 rpm, the 5.0-liter, F1-inspired V-10 in this M5 produced 500 horsepower and 380 lb-ft of torque. Its subtle and classy exterior makes this V-10-powered super sedan one hell of a sleeper. The M5 wasn't the only BMW M car to receive that magnificent 5.0-liter V-10. The big-boy, two-door M6 got the same engine, paired to either a seven-speed single-clutch automated manual or a traditional six-speed. Both are sure to cost you dearly to maintain, but it’s hard to complain too much after listening to its incredible soundtrack. In keeping the German super-sedan theme going, we present the Audi S8. It uses a 5.2-liter Lamborghini-related V-10 to haul its 4300-pound body to 60 mph in 4.8 seconds. The tuxedo-trim good looks and everyday usability made this car an excellent balance between work and play. If it wasn’t clear by now, you can tell the VW Group made good use of its V-10 from this era. The only pickup truck on this list is a banger. This is the Dodge Ram SRT-10, a two-door Ram with a wing and a gargantuan 8.3-liter naturally aspirated V-10 borrowed from the Viper. You could even get it with a manual transmission. It remains the ultimate performance truck to this day, but Ram is coming for its own crown with the Hellcat-powered Rumblebee launching next year. How cool is a diesel-powered V-10? Cool enough for U.S. emissions regulations to cancel the Touareg TDI's sales here (twice). Twin turbos aid the ten cylinders, and the engine produces 310 horsepower and 553 lb-ft of torque. Besides this Volkswagen, the only other V-10-powered SUV made was the Ford Excursion, making it an extremely rare breed. VW IS MULLING A NEW FLAGSHIP SUV FOR A MORE AFFLUENT CROWD The McLaren Solus GT is the by far the newest V-10-powered car on this list. It's a track-only special with a unique 5.2-liter engine that revs to 10,000 rpm and has 829 horsepower and 479 lb-ft of torque. Thanks to its slim single-seater design and carbon fiber monocoque, it weighs just 2205 pounds. It’s an absolute rocketship. title: Between stadiums, BTS' V turns to a book on quiet power of everyday life - The Korea Herald
content:
Published : July 27, 2026 - 17:46:03
Updated : July 29, 2026 - 10:43:29 Between stadium performances and global commitments, BTS' V has drawn attention to a book that explores the quiet power of simply getting through everyday life. Late Thursday night, the singer shared on his Instagram story "The Sensibility of an Everyday Person" (a literal translation of the Korean title), a newly published essay collection by the celebrated Korean lyricist Kim Eana. The publisher, Storyseller, said messages poured in almost immediately after V shared the book. "Seeing the response the moment V shared the book reminded us just how much it means to authors and publishers when an artist introduces the books that have inspired them," the publisher wrote on social media. Kim reposted V's story on Instagram with a brief note of thanks addressed to the singer by his given name, Kim Tae-hyung. One of South Korea's most influential lyricists, Kim Eana has written some of modern K-pop's defining songs, including Park Hyo-shin's poignant ballad "Breath," Brown Eyed Girls' era-defining dance hit "Abracadabra," IU's breakthrough anthem "Good Day" and Ive's self-affirming chart-topper "I Am." If self-help books often promise reinvention, Kim's latest collection argues for something more modest: returning to the rhythms of everyday life. Kim described the book as an exploration of "the small things that saved me when everyday life felt close enough to touch but somehow remained out of reach, when life seemed ever so slightly out of alignment and I felt alone in it." Kim turns her attention to those quietly sustaining an ordinary life. The essays offer comfort to readers who are simply trying to get through each day. "The days that unfold without dramatic highs or lows, without straying from their course, are proof that we're living earnestly," she writes. "How much time and effort does it take to simply keep that going?" Kim writes that finding happiness in such ordinary things is "a tremendous blessing." While everyone naturally strives for a better material life, the quality of that life ultimately depends on whether we have "small moments of happiness we can savor like pieces of candy along the way." The new collection is her first book in six years, following her 2020 bestseller "Ordinary Words," which has sold more than 200,000 copies. V's recommendation arrives as BTS enters another busy stretch. After wrapping up the European leg of its "Arirang" world tour, the group is set to begin performances across North and South America on Aug. 1.
